article.title: Editing utterance-final particles by function and context
article.chapter: Norma, estilo y elección avanzada C2 — 規範、文體與進階選擇 C2

claims.sectionKey: Qué muestran los recursos y estudios
claims.summary: The Sinica Taiwan Mandarin Conversational Corpus is a 43-hour resource with free, topic-specific, and Map Task conversations; transcripts annotate particles and discourse markers, while only MCDC8 has manual Pinyin/POS checking and other corpora are automatically processed.

claims.sectionKey: Qué muestran los recursos y estudios
claims.summary: Tseng and Yeong analyzed 24 online classes with 15 preservice teachers and six learners; utterance-final particles occurred in 15% of student turns and 37% of teacher turns in that sample, and the authors note speaker/background and relationship factors.

Checking speaker, addressee, interaction context, corpus genre, and annotation before judging a particle's frequency or editing it is a limited editorial inference from the corpus design and study's observed contextual variation; neither source establishes a correct universal frequency or deletion rule.

The Sinica resource documents conversational Taiwan Mandarin and the Tseng and Yeong study analyzes online pedagogical interactions; their results do not establish overuse in academic prose or all conversation.

links.notes: The institute's corpus guide gives duration, design and speakers; it says particles are annotated and distinguishes manually checked from automatically processed data.
The study record at National Taiwan Normal University reproduces authors, DOI, sample, turn-level proportions and factors associated with frequency.
Multiple conversation scenarios and explicit annotation cautions support checking genre and annotation before drawing conclusions from corpus counts.
The authors identify interaction, regional and language-background factors; the editorial check is explicitly a limited inference, not a published prescription.
The resource is a spoken conversational corpus and distinguishes different scenarios and processing quality.
The study sample is teacher-student online interactions and the authors describe participant/context factors; it is not evidence about all registers.
